items.title: Turn Indigo data into two use cases
items.text:
Work in pairs. Choose two decisions Indigo could improve with the course datasets. For each one, identify the goal, the data that would be available at prediction time, and an action the team could take.

Two good starting points are available in the current data:

Use case Dataset and target Possible action Estimate which website visits may lead to a purchase website_analytics.csv; predict purchased Offer checkout help before a visitor completes a purchase Recommend another product to a returning customer sales.csv; use past customer-product purchases Suggest a product that similar customers bought

The website file has about 11,000 visits and about 1,000 purchases, enough for a classroom classification exercise. The sales file has nearly 1,000 customers and 30 products, enough for a small recommendation prototype.

Keep the prediction honest

Do not give a model information that would only be known after the outcome. For website purchase prediction, leave out transaction_id. This starter uses stock availability and cart activity, both known before checkout completes. Traffic source and promotion are possible extensions; use visit duration only if it is measured at the moment the team plans to act. A purchase record is a clue about interest, not proof of preference.

items.title: Install scikit-learn
items.text:
Open the terminal in your indigo-data project and add the package:

uv add scikit-learn

If you do not have the course CSV files in your project yet, download them from the Indigo data page and place them in a data folder.

items.title: Start with purchase prediction
items.text:
This small baseline uses logistic regression to predict whether a website visit led to a purchase. It compares the model with a simple baseline that always predicts “no purchase”.

import polars as pl
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

visits = pl.read_csv("data/website_analytics.csv")

features = (
    visits.select("product_available", "added_to_cart")
    .with_columns(
        pl.col("product_available").cast(pl.Int8),
        pl.col("added_to_cart").cast(pl.Int8),
    )
    .to_numpy()
)
target = visits.get_column("purchased").cast(pl.Int8).to_numpy()

x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    features, target, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=target
)

baseline = DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent")
baseline.fit(x_train, y_train)
print("Always no purchase")
print(classification_report(y_test, baseline.predict(x_test), zero_division=0))

model = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced", max_iter=1000),
)
model.fit(x_train, y_train)
print("Logistic regression")
print(classification_report(y_test, model.predict(x_test), zero_division=0))

purchased is unevenly distributed, so accuracy alone can hide missed purchases. Compare precision (how often a purchase prediction is right) and recall (how many actual purchases the model finds). Decide which matters more for the action Indigo would take.

items.title: Build a product recommender
items.text:
Use sales.csv to make a customer-by-product table: each row is a customer, each column is a product, and a cell records whether that customer bought it. Then use sklearn.neighbors.NearestNeighbors with cosine distance to find customers with similar purchase histories.

Your recommendation must omit products the customer already bought. Test it by holding out each customer's most recent new product, making recommendations from earlier purchases, and checking how often the held-out product appears near the top. Compare against recommending the most popular products to everyone.

What should the team deliver?

For each use case, show the business question, target or recommendation, input columns, one model, one baseline, and one evaluation result. End with one sentence describing the action Indigo could take and one limitation of the data.

About the product data

This dataset is simulated and has no product impressions or customer demographics. It can support a classroom recommendation prototype for the existing 30 products. It cannot show whether a real customer saw an item, explain why they liked it, or reliably recommend Indigo's new refillable shampoo before that product has purchase history.

items.title: Question to a model
items.text:
In marketing, many questions look like this:

  • which customers are the most likely to churn?
  • which products should we suggest to customers?
  • who should we target for our ad campaign?

In data / machine learning, those problems can be (partially?) solve using prediction techniques, especially with machine learning models. Those models look for patterns in examples, and for this we need:

  • Target: which is the thing we want it to predict: probability of churn, expected spend, etc
  • Features: anything that can help us predict our target: time since subscribed, age, buying behaviors, etc

Important

In all of the examples below, all visualization are in 2d (or 3d), because otherwise we wouldn't be able to represent them. This means that we only have 1 or 2 features, but keep in mind that in the real world we often use much more features.

items.title: Linear regression
items.text:
Linear regression is the most simple machine learning model. It uses a line to estimate a number.

PlaygroundHow it works

Each dot represents a customer's age and monthly spending. The model finds a straight line that stays close to the examples, then uses that line to estimate spending for a new customer.

graph LR
  examples[Past customers] --> line[Find the trend in a straight line]
  age[New customer's age] --> line
  line --> estimate[Estimated monthly spending]

items.title: Train-test split
items.text:
When we create a model, we need to find a way to evaluate it. Let's say we have a model that predicts the spending of a customer next month. We use that model every month to know how much money we expect to make.

How can we know whether that value is accurate or not?

For this, we often split our dataset into 2 sets: a train set and the test set.

items.title: Logistic regression
items.text:
Estimate the probability of one of two outcomes, such as a purchase or no purchase. The threshold controls when a probability becomes a positive prediction.

PlaygroundHow it works

The model learns which customer traits tend to go with a purchase, then estimates a purchase probability for each new customer. A threshold turns that probability into a yes-or-no prediction. A lower threshold reaches more people, while a higher one focuses on the most likely buyers.

graph LR
  history[Past customer behavior and purchases] --> model[Learn purchase patterns]
  customer[New customer's behavior] --> model
  model --> probability[Estimated purchase probability]
  probability --> threshold{Above the campaign threshold?}
  threshold -->|Yes| target[Include in campaign]
  threshold -->|No| skip[Do not include]

items.title: Decision trees
items.text:
A tree asks a sequence of simple questions about the features. Greater depth can capture more detail, but can also fit noise in the examples.

PlaygroundHow it works

At each decision point, or node , the tree tries possible cutoffs on its features, such as fewer or more product visits. It chooses a cutoff that leaves the resulting groups with less mixing between purchasers and non-purchasers, then repeats the process inside each group.

A group where the tree stops asking questions is a leaf . It predicts the purchase likelihood from the share of training customers in that group who purchased.

The maximum depth sets how many questions can appear along a path from the top of the tree to a leaf. The minimum examples per group sets how many training customers each side of a split must contain. In this playground, the defaults are depth 4 and 6 examples per group. A group stops splitting when it reaches the depth limit, contains only one outcome, or cannot be divided while keeping the minimum examples on both sides. Increasing the depth allows more detailed rules; increasing the minimum group size favors broader rules.

graph TD
  start{Visited the product page?}
  start -->|Yes| email{Opened a recent email?}
  start -->|No| unlikely[Less likely to purchase]
  email -->|Yes| likely[More likely to purchase]
  email -->|No| unsure[Less likely to purchase]
  classDef leaf fill:#e4f3e8,stroke:#3a7d44,color:#1f3d23,stroke-width:2px
  class unlikely,likely,unsure leaf

items.title: Random forests
items.text:
A forest combines predictions from many decision trees trained on slightly different samples. Compare a small forest with a larger one and change how deep each tree can grow.

PlaygroundHow it works

A random forest builds many decision trees, each using a slightly different sample of customers. The trees each make a prediction, and the forest combines their votes. This makes the result less dependent on the quirks of any one tree.

graph LR
  customers[Past customers] --> sample1[Sample of customers]
  customers --> sample2[Another sample]
  customers --> sample3[Another sample]
  sample1 --> tree1[Tree 1 vote]
  sample2 --> tree2[Tree 2 vote]
  sample3 --> tree3[Tree 3 vote]
  tree1 --> combine[Combine the votes]
  tree2 --> combine
  tree3 --> combine
  combine --> prediction[Forest prediction]

items.title: K-nearest neighbors
items.text:
K-nearest neighbors looks at the most similar examples nearby. Change the number of neighbors and click the chart to ask the model about a new point.

PlaygroundHow it works

K is the number of nearby examples used to make a prediction. When you click the chart, the model measures the straight-line distance from that point to the plotted examples and selects the K closest. It estimates the purchase likelihood from the share of those neighbors who purchased. For example, with K = 7, if 5 of the neighbors purchased, the estimate is 5 out of 7, or about 71%.

A small K makes the prediction depend on a very local group, so one unusual example can change it. A larger K includes a wider neighborhood and tends to make predictions smoother, though examples farther away can influence the result. The playground lets you compare odd values from 1 to 31; odd values avoid a tied vote between two outcomes.

graph LR
  new[New customer] --> find[Find K closest examples]
  past[Past customers and their purchases] --> find
  find --> neighbors[Example: K = 7; 5 purchased, 2 did not]
  neighbors --> vote[Purchase likelihood: 5 out of 7]
  vote --> prediction[About 71%]

items.title: Data
items.text:
Any information that can be collected, stored, and analyzed

In practice, we often separate tabular and non-tabular data.

TabularNon-tabular

Can fit into a table or a spreadsheet

  • Numerical: prices, temperatures, revenue, sensor measurements, ages, time spent, number of clicks, etc.
  • Categorical: country, product category, customer type, yes/no values, etc.
  • Time-series: stock prices, website traffic, heart rate measurements, IoT readings over time.
  • Graph/network: social connections, relationships between companies, transportation networks.
  • Location/spatial: GPS coordinates, maps, geographic regions.

Everything else

  • Text: emails, reviews, documents, social media posts, support conversations.
  • Images: photographs, medical scans, satellite imagery, handwritten digits.
  • Audio: speech recordings, music, environmental sounds.
  • Video: surveillance footage, sports recordings, driving footage.

items.title: Big data
items.text:
Big data describes data whose scale, speed, diversity, or complexity creates challenges for traditional tools and processes. A common way to remember the challenges is the "3 Vs" (sometimes 5):

Meaning Example Volume A lot of records Millions of website events Velocity Data arrives quickly or continuously Live clicks during a product launch Variety Many formats and sources Tables, reviews, images, video, and sensor data

Big data is not automatically valuable. A large dataset can still be irrelevant, biased, badly collected, or impossible to interpret.

items.title: Smart data
items.text:
Smart data is a practical label for data that has been selected, prepared, contextualised, and governed so that it can support a specific decision. It is not necessarily large.

For a campaign, a small table containing recent, consented, relevant customer segments may be more useful than billions of unfiltered social-media events. Smart data should be:

  • relevant to the question
  • understandable, with clear definitions and units
  • timely enough for the decision
  • checked for quality and bias
  • collected and used lawfully
  • connected to an action or decision.

items.title: Open data
items.text:
Open data is data that people can access, use, and share under stated conditions, usually through an open licence. "Open" does not mean "anything is allowed": a licence can require attribution, prohibit certain uses, or specify how the data can be shared.

Open data in France

In France, a lot of data is made public via the data.gouv.fr platform. There are a lot of things you can find: businesses and the economy, real estate and urban planning, geography and addresses, transport and mobility, energy and the environment, health, education, employment and population, agriculture and food, public administration and finance, elections and public life, culture, and security.

items.title: Data in AI vs AI
items.text:
What we call "AI" often means generative AI, but AI is much more than that.

flowchart TB
    A["Rule-Based Systems<br/>1950s–1980s<br/>IF / ELSE • Expert Systems"]
    B["Early Learning Algorithms<br/>1950s–1990s<br/>Perceptron • Decision Trees"]
    C["Machine Learning<br/>1990s–2010s<br/>SVM • Random Forests • Statistical Learning"]
    D["Deep Learning<br/>2010s<br/>Neural Networks • CNNs • RNNs • Transformers"]
    E["Generative AI<br/>2020s–Today<br/>LLMs • Diffusion Models • Multimodal AI"]

    A -->|"Rules → Learning from data"| B
    B -->|"Better algorithms + more data"| C
    C -->|"Large datasets + GPUs"| D
    D -->|"Foundation models"| E

Today, most people doing data analytics aren't doing AI, but all AI researchers/engineers are working with data.

The rise of Gen AI has been possible mostly because of compute availability:

We're now using an extremely high amount of compute, and even more each year:

items.title: Jobs
items.text:
Data work is collaborative. Job titles vary between organisations, and one person may perform several roles in a small company.

Role Main responsibility Chief Data Officer (CDO) Connects data strategy, governance, and business priorities Data engineer Builds and maintains systems that collect, move, and store data Data analyst Explores and summarises data to answer business questions Data scientist Uses statistics, machine learning, and programming to model patterns or make predictions Data Protection Officer (DPO) Advises on privacy, data protection obligations, rights, and governance

In practice, many of those job titles are mixed together and companies often don't make true differences between them. Also,

items.text:
In 2017, Google researchers published a now extremely famous paper titled Attention is all you need, presenting the Transformer architecture.

items.title: An LLM isn't a database
items.text:
It might feel natural to compare an LLM to a search tool like Google, but they are very different. An LLM is literally one (or multiple) file(s) stored somewhere. It contains between dozens of millions of parameters (see example below) and hundreds of billions of parameters (Claude, ChatGPT, etc.).

Here is an AI running completely "offline". Once it says "Ready!", you can:

  • turn off your wifi
  • try to chat with it

Warning

  • Don't refresh the page, otherwise it won't work
  • This might slow down your computer a little bit

Tip

Everything you ask the AI here is 100% private. Nobody, not even the instructor, could ever know what you ask it.

As you run some tests, you'll see that:

  • answers are kind of weird and not very clear
  • it often stops mid-sentence

The latter is because, at each step when making predictions, the model computes what the next word in that sentence will be (or token, as we should say). Its reasoning is basically something like this:

  • Given all tokens so far, it computes a probability distribution over the possible next tokens. In the sentence "I hope I'll have a good [...]", the LLM tries to figure out what "[...]" could be. It is likely to predict something like a 40% chance of "day", a 30% chance of "morning", etc.
  • A token is selected from that distribution: it could be the one with the highest chance (e.g., "day") or some more sophisticated method.
  • That token is appended to the context: the sentence becomes "I hope I'll have a good day [...]".
  • And the process repeats.
  • Generation stops when the model produces a special end-of-sequence (EOS) token, or when some external stopping condition is reached (such as a maximum token limit).

items.title: Before Gen AI
items.text:
As we said before, there was "AI" long before "Generative AI", and non-generative AI still exists today. The process is exactly the same:

  • gather a lot of data. In practice, it's often just user data.
  • train an AI model on it for a specific task.
  • evaluate that model
  • make inferences with it

The list could be much longer, but the following are the most common use cases:

fraud detectionrecommendation systemsmedical image analysischurn prediction

Detects suspicious transactions or unusual behavior that may indicate fraud, such as stolen credit cards or unauthorized payments.

Predicts what content or products a user is most likely to be interested in based on their behavior, preferences, and similar users. This is used, for example, by YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Vinted, ...

Analyzes medical images such as X-rays, MRIs, or CT scans to help identify abnormalities, diseases, or other relevant patterns.

Predicts which customers are likely to stop using a product or service, allowing companies to take action to retain them.

Most of those uses fall into the two main categories:

  • regression: predict a number (e.g., how much ice cream we need at this store next week)
  • classification: predict a category (e.g., does this patient have a tumor or not?) or a probability (e.g., what are the odds of this patient having a tumor?)

Question

In your opinion, does an LLM do regression or classification?

items.title: Indigo
items.text:
Indigo

For this course, we'll assume that we work for the marketing department of Indigo, a company selling organic cleaning products. Indigo wants to launch a new refillable shampoo product.

We want to answer questions such as:

  • Who might be interested in the product in the current customer base?
  • Which message and channel should we use?
  • How should we price that product?
  • What are customers saying about the product?
  • What does that teach us about launching a new product?

items.title: Schema
items.text:
flowchart LR
  products[Products] -->|product_id| sales[Sales]
  products -->|product_id| visits[Website analytics]
  products -->|product_id| reviews[Product reviews]
  promotions[Promotions] -->|promotion_code| campaigns[Marketing campaigns]
  promotions -->|promotion_code| visits
  promotions -->|promotion_code| sales
  campaigns -->|send_id = campaign_send_id| visits
  campaigns -->|send_id = campaign_send_id| sales
  visits -->|transaction_id| sales
  campaigns -->|transaction_id| sales
  sales -->|transaction_id| reviews

items.title: Datasets
items.text:
SalesWebsite analyticsProduct reviewsMarketing campaignsProductsPromotions

One row represents a completed transaction. transaction_id is its unique ID. gross_total is the list-price total before discounts; transaction_total is after discounts and before refunds; net_total is after refunds. discount_amount, refund_amount, returned_quantity, return_status, and return_date describe discounts and returns. sales_channel identifies other sales, website sales, or campaign-attributed sales. campaign_send_id and visit_id connect attributed sales to their originating events.

One row represents a product-page visit. It includes 10,000 ordinary visits and sessions created from campaign clicks. time_spent is the session duration in seconds. product_available records whether the item was in stock at the start of the visit. A completed purchase has a transaction_id that joins to Sales. Campaign sessions also carry campaign_send_id, which joins to Marketing campaigns.

One row represents a review of a purchased product. transaction_id joins the review to the sale, and the customer and product IDs match that transaction. The review date is on or after the purchase date. Text varies in length, tone, spelling, casing, and punctuation, including very positive and very negative opinions.

One row represents a campaign message sent to a customer. Each experiment_id is an A/B message test within one campaign. Recipients are randomly assigned to message_variant A or B, with the assignment kept consistent for that customer in that campaign; both variants share the campaign's channel, offer, and period. Variant B has a small simulated lift in clicks and purchases. Compare click and purchase rates by experiment and variant. promotion_code joins to Promotions. A click has a visit_id linking to Website analytics, and its time_spent value in seconds matches that session. When purchased is true, transaction_id joins to Sales and amount_purchased equals that transaction's discounted total before refunds.

One row represents a product. product_id joins to sales, website visits, and reviews. list_price is in euros and is the price before promotions. opening_stock is available at the start of 2025; monthly_restock_quantity is added at the start of each following month. Sales cannot exceed available stock, and website visits record whether the product was available.

One row represents a promotion code. discount_rate is the fraction taken off the product's list price, and the active dates show when the code can be used. Campaign-specific offers also include a campaign_id. Promotion codes join to Marketing campaigns, Website analytics, and Sales.

items.title: Pair activity
items.text:
Choose one of the case questions and work with a partner.

  1. Write the decision the team wants to make.
  2. List three pieces of data that could help.
  3. For each piece, write where it could come from.
  4. Add one reason the data might be incomplete, misleading, or inappropriate.

Do not confuse a proxy with the thing itself

A click is a record of clicking, not proof that someone read, liked, remembered, or believed a message. A purchase is evidence of a transaction, not a complete explanation of motivation nor a happy customer.

items.title: What each tool does
items.text: Tool Explanation Python A programming language that we will use in later sessions to work with data Positron The application where you open projects, notebooks, data, and results uv A tool that installs Python versions and packages and keeps a project's environment organised

items.title: Step 1: install Positron
items.text:
1. Open the official Positron download page.
  2. Download the installer for your operating system.
  3. Install and open Positron.

items.title: Step 2: check or install uv
items.text:
Mac/LinuxWindows PowerShell

Open the Terminal application and paste:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

Open the PowerShell application and paste:

irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex

To verify it's actually installed:

  1. In Positron, open View > Terminal.
  2. Type the command below and press Enter.
uv --version

If a version number appears, uv is ready.

The official uv installation page lists alternative installation methods.

If installation is restricted

You do not need administrator rights for every installation method. If your network blocks the installer, continue with a neighbour and tell the instructor.

items.title: Step 3: create a project environment
items.text:
The Positron menus may look slightly different across versions, but the workflow is the same.

  1. In Positron, choose New > New Folder from Template.
  2. Select Python Project.
  3. Choose a location such as your Documents folder and name the project indigo-data.
  4. When asked, create a pyproject.toml file.
  5. Choose Create a new virtual environment.
  6. Choose uv as the environment provider (default).
  7. Name the environment .venv (default).
  8. Choose the latest stable Python version offered by Positron, then select Create.

Positron may download Python through uv if Python is not already installed. This is expected. A new .venv folder should appear in the project, along with a pyproject.toml file.

items.title: Step 4: install one package and verify it can be used
items.text:
We will install polars, a common package for working with tables.

  1. Make sure the Positron terminal is open in the indigo-data project.
  2. Go to Terminal:
uv add polars

The command adds the package to the project and updates the project's environment. It should also record the dependency in pyproject.toml.

  1. Go to Console.
  2. Copy the following code block, paste it, and press Enter:
import sys
import polars as pl

print(sys.executable)
print(sys.version)
print(pl.__version__)

You have succeeded when the cell prints a Python path, a Python version, and a polars version without errors.

Troubleshooting

uv is not found: close and reopen the terminal, then try uv --version again. If it still fails, use the official uv installation page or ask for help.

The .venv environment does not appear: open the Command Palette and run Interpreter: Discover All Interpreters, then select the .venv environment.

The notebook uses the wrong environment: click the kernel selector at the top of the notebook and choose the interpreter inside your project's .venv folder.

The package installation fails: check your internet connection and the spelling of uv add polars. If the computer is managed by your school or company, ask the instructor rather than changing security settings yourself.

For more detail, see Positron's Python installation and environment guide and first Python notebook tutorial.

items.title: What does "clean" mean?
items.text:
Data cleaning makes a dataset more consistent and useful for a specific question. Poor quality can distort a campaign comparison, hide an operational issue, or lead a team to act on the wrong customers. In practice, we want to make the data "tidy".

In the previous lesson, we saw common ways to clean data (selecting columns, filtering rows, and aggregating). Here we'll talk about common issues that arise when cleaning data, why they occur, and how to "fix" them (if they need fixing).

items.title: Definitions
items.text:
completely at randomat randomnot at randomby design

Data is missing for purely random reasons. This is the ideal case, since ignoring those values has no impact on our analysis, but it is almost never the case in the real world.

A bank with customer info might be missing information about its customers' jobs. It's likely that people who don't want to share their job have reasons: a bad credit score, illegal activities, ...

Missingness isn't random and can be explained by other variables.

Men are less likely to receive a diagnosis of depression, but this has nothing to do with their level of depression. Statistics allow us to easily account for sex.

Data is not missing at random when the value of the missing variable is related to the reason it's missing. People with severe symptoms of depression are more likely not to answer questions because of their symptoms.

When sending marketing emails, a blank value for time spent on the website isn't really missing data if a user didn't click the link to the website. Want to know how much time users spend on your website on average after clicking through from your email campaign? Start by filtering for users who clicked through, and you'll "remove" missing values.

items.title: Exercise
items.text:
For each scenario, decide whether the data is completely at random, at random, not at random, or missing by design. Open each card to check your answer.

A sensor loses readings during randomly timed transmission glitches

The glitches affect readings across devices and times, with no connection to the recorded conditions or the readings themselves. What kind of missing data is this?

Answer: completely at random. The missingness has no relationship to observed variables or to the missing readings.

A customer survey does not ask for household income

Customers with higher incomes are more likely to skip the income question. What kind of missing data is this?

Answer: not at random. Whether income is missing is related to the income value itself.

A satisfaction score is missing more often in one app version

A bug in the survey form affects the oldest app version. The app version is recorded for every customer. What kind of missing data is this?

Answer: at random. Missingness is related to an observed variable, the app version, rather than to the satisfaction score itself.

A delivery time is blank for orders that were never shipped

The dataset records a delivery time only after an order has shipped. What kind of missing data is this?

Answer: by design. A delivery time does not exist for an order that was never shipped, so the blank is not an unrecorded value.

A health question is skipped more often by older respondents

Age is recorded for everyone, and older respondents are more likely to leave the question blank. What kind of missing data is this?

Answer: at random. The missingness can be explained by the observed age variable.

items.title: Outliers
items.text:
Let's look at graduates' annual income ten years after graduation.

What should the school publish?

The mean includes everyone but can be pulled up by one $500,000 income. The median may better represent a typical graduate. If you exclude a valid outcome, say so clearly.

items.title: Exercise
items.text: In this exercise, you'll investigate six outlier cases and figure out what should be done in each one.

items.title: Polars crash course
items.text: In this course we'll use polars, a famous dataframe library. It's open source (the entire underlying code is freely available online) and completely free.

items.title: Why not just use Excel?
items.text:
Excel is a bit more accessible than writing code when it comes to manipulating data because everything is very visual and interactive. Thing is, this also comes with important limitations:

  • 1M-row limit in Excel: insanely low
  • It's not meant for automation, reproducibility, scalability, composability, or integration

  • Commercial software:

    • you need a Microsoft licence
    • you don't own your work
    • your data isn't private

Note

Those limitations are approximately the same for alternative products such as Google Sheets.

With programming tools (especially polars), working with 100 or 100M rows doesn't make such a big difference. polars will stay free forever, and you don't depend on any entity.

The #1 reason people use Excel is that it is (or rather, seems) simpler to use. But in the AI era, coding has become dramatically more accessible, especially if you know what you're doing, which is required no matter which tool you use.

Instead, the best investment you could make is to understand how polars works in general and work with AI to handle the rest. You'll never have privacy, performance, automation, or scalability issues.

items.title: Read files
items.text:
Reading a file is like opening an Excel spreadsheet.

ExampleExerciseHint 
import polars as pl

# We read the CSV file and create a "sales" dataframe
sales = pl.read_csv("src/data_analytics_and_AI/data/sales.csv")

items.title: Select data
items.text:
Use select to choose the columns you need. Keeping a small set of relevant columns makes a table easier to inspect and share.

ExampleExerciseHint 
import polars as pl

# Read the sales dataset
sales = pl.read_csv("src/data_analytics_and_AI/data/sales.csv")

# Select 3 columns
overview = sales.select("transaction_id", "date", "net_total")

# Print the first 5 rows
print(overview.head())

│ transaction_id ┆ date       ┆ net_total │
│ ---            ┆ ---        ┆ ---       │

Select the product_name, quantity, and net_total columns from sales. Store the result in a variable named product_sales and print its first five rows.

  • Pass each column name to sales.select(...), then use .head() to show a few rows. Column names are case-sensitive and must match the CSV header.
  • When unsure about column names, you can either click on the CSV file in Positron, or run print(sales.columns).

items.title: Filter rows
items.text:
Use filter to keep rows that match a condition. pl.col("column") refers to a column, and comparisons such as ==, >, and != create conditions. Combine conditions with & for “and” or | for “or”; put parentheses around each condition.

ExampleExerciseHint 
import polars as pl

# Read the dataset
sales = pl.read_csv("src/data_analytics_and_AI/data/sales.csv")

# Keep transactions with an amount greater than €100
high_value_sales = sales.filter(pl.col("net_total") > 100)

# Print the first few rows
print(high_value_sales.select("transaction_id", "product_name", "net_total").head())

│ transaction_id ┆ product_name    ┆ net_total │

│ T000020        ┆ Urban Bottle 27 ┆ 102.64    │

Keep only sales where sales_channel is "online". Store the result in online_sales, then print its first five rows.

Compare the column expression with the string value: pl.col("sales_channel") == "online". Put that condition inside sales.filter(...).

items.title: Group by
items.text:
Use group_by to collect rows with the same value, then agg to calculate a summary for each group. Common aggregations include .sum(), .mean(), and .len().

ExampleExerciseHint 
import polars as pl

# Read the sales dataset
sales = pl.read_csv("src/data_analytics_and_AI/data/sales.csv")

# Group by sales channel and compute total sales for each one
sales_agg = sales.group_by("sales_channel").agg(net_revenue=pl.col("net_total").sum())

# Print the result (no need for head() here since there are just 3 channels)
print(sales_agg)

shape: (3, 2)
┌────────────────────┬─────────────┐
│ sales_channel      ┆ net_revenue │
│ ---                ┆ ---         │
│ str                ┆ f64         │
╞════════════════════╪═════════════╡
│ other              ┆ 456582.99   │
│ website            ┆ 75062.63    │
│ marketing_campaign ┆ 10476.42    │
└────────────────────┴─────────────┘

Group the sales by product_name and calculate the total quantity sold for each product. Name the total column units_sold, then sort the result by units_sold from highest to lowest.

Start with sales.group_by("product_name"), then aggregate with pl.col("quantity").sum().alias("units_sold").

items.title: Expressions
items.text:
A Polars expression describes a calculation using one or more columns. Use pl.col("column") to refer to a column, then combine expressions with arithmetic or methods such as .sum(). Polars evaluates the expression inside an operation such as with_columns, select, or agg.

ExampleExerciseHint 
import polars as pl

sales = pl.read_csv("src/data_analytics_and_AI/data/sales.csv")
sales_with_discount = sales.with_columns(
    (pl.col("list_unit_price") - pl.col("unit_price")).alias("discount_per_unit")
)
print(sales_with_discount.select("product_name", "discount_per_unit").head())

│ Bright Organizer 13 ┆ 0.0               │
│ Essential Bag 28    ┆ 4.9               │
└─────────────────────┴───────────────────┘

Create a new line_total column by multiplying quantity by unit_price. Store the result in sales_with_line_total and print the product_name and line_total columns for the first five rows.

Inside with_columns(...), multiply pl.col("quantity") by pl.col("unit_price"). Use .alias("line_total") to give the calculated column its name.

items.title: Chaining operations
items.text:
Each Polars operation returns a DataFrame that the next operation can use. Chaining lets you filter rows, select columns, and then group and summarize the remaining data in one readable sequence.

ExampleExerciseHint 
import polars as pl

sales = pl.read_csv("src/data_analytics_and_AI/data/sales.csv")
online_revenue = (
    sales.group_by("sales_channel")      # For each sales channel
    .agg(pl.col("net_total").sum())      # Compute total of sales
    .sort("net_total", descending=True)  # And sort them by amount
)
print(online_revenue)

┌────────────────────┬───────────┐
│ sales_channel      ┆ net_total │
│ ---                ┆ ---       │
│ str                ┆ f64       │
╞════════════════════╪═══════════╡
│ other              ┆ 456582.99 │
│ website            ┆ 75062.63  │
│ marketing_campaign ┆ 10476.42  │
└────────────────────┴───────────┘

Chain operations to keep online sales, select the product_name and quantity columns, then group by product and calculate total units sold. Name the result units_sold and print the final table.

Begin with sales.filter(...), follow it with .select(...), then .group_by("product_name").agg(...). The filter condition is pl.col("sales_channel") == "online".

items.title: Python crash course
items.text:
In the next lesson, we'll use Python, one of the world's most famous programming languages. This page introduces the basic ideas you'll need to read and write small Python programs.

Warning

  • Make sure you've installed Positron and uv (see the guide if not).
  • The goal isn't to make you a programming expert! Instead, I want you to grasp the core concepts of manipulating data with code, learn to do basic operations, and then learn how to use AI to do them for you.

items.title: Get ready
items.text:
We'll write Python in Positron and use uv to run it. uv can create a starter script and run it without adding any packages.

ExampleExerciseHint
  • Open a new folder in Positron.
  • Create a main.py file
  • Open main.py, replace its contents with the code below, and save it.
  • Either select the code and hit "Run", or open a terminal and run uv run main.py
print("Hello, Python!")

Replace the message with one that introduces you. Save main.py and run uv run main.py again to see the change.

print("Hello, Python!")

Text that you want Python to display goes inside quotation marks and parentheses: print("your message").

items.title: Read code from top to bottom
items.text:
Python runs each line in order, from the top of the file to the bottom. A comment starts with #; Python skips it, so you can leave notes for people reading your code.

ExampleExerciseHint 
# I can write anything here!
print("Preparing data")
print("Let's get started")

Run this starter code. Add a second print statement below the first so it also displays Ready to explore, then run it again.

# Python runs these lines from top to bottom
print("Sales data")
# TODO: display "Ready to explore"

Put each message in its own print(...) call. The line order determines which message appears first.

items.title: Store values in variables
items.text:
A variable gives a name to a value so you can use it later. Use = to assign a value.

ExampleExerciseHint 
product_name = "Notebook"
quantity = 3
unit_price = 4.50

print(product_name)
print(quantity)
print(unit_price)

Change the three values to describe a product of your choice. Run the code and check that it prints the values you assigned.

product_name = "Notebook"
quantity = 3
unit_price = 4.50

print(product_name)
print(quantity)
print(unit_price)

Put text in quotes, and write numbers without quotes. Choose clear names such as product_name and unit_price.

items.title: Calculate with values
items.text:
Python can calculate with numbers. The basic operators are + for addition, - for subtraction, * for multiplication, and / for division. Store a calculation in a variable to use its result later.

ExampleExerciseHint 
quantity = 3
unit_price = 4.50
line_total = quantity * unit_price

print(line_total)

Complete the calculation so total is the price of five items. Run the code and check the result.

quantity = 5
unit_price = 2.25

# TODO: multiply quantity by unit_price and store the result in total
total = 0
print(total)

Multiply the quantity by the unit price with *: 5 * 2.25.

items.title: Work with text
items.text:
Text values are called strings. You can join strings with +, or use an f-string to insert values into a sentence. An f-string starts with f before the opening quote; put each variable inside braces.

ExampleExerciseHint 
product_name = "Notebook"
quantity = 3
print(f"We sold {quantity} {product_name}s.")

Change the values, then replace the TODO with an f-string that prints the product name and price. Run the code to check the sentence.

product_name = "Notebook"
unit_price = 4.50

# TODO: print a sentence that includes both values

Start the text with f and put each variable name inside {}. For example: f"The price is {unit_price}".

items.title: Python's basic types
items.text:
Every value has a type, which determines what you can do with it. The main types you'll use here are int for whole numbers, float for decimal numbers, str for text, and bool for either True or False. Use type(...) to inspect a value's type.

Numbers can be added to other numbers, including an int and a float. Strings can be joined with other strings, but Python won't add a number to a string. Convert a number with str(...) when you want to include it in text. Comparisons such as > produce a boolean, and and, or, and not combine boolean values.

Example 
quantity = 3                 # int
unit_price = 4.50            # float
product_name = "Notebook"    # str
is_available = True          # bool

total = quantity * unit_price
message = "Total: " + str(total)
can_purchase = is_available and quantity > 0

print(type(quantity))
print(type(unit_price))
print(type(product_name))
print(type(is_available))
print(message)
print(can_purchase)

Warning

"Total: " + total raises a TypeError because total is a number and "Total: " is text. Convert the number with str(total), or use an f-string such as f"Total: {total}".

Tip

Python has many other types, some of which are described below.

items.title: Keep several values in a list
items.text:
A list stores values in order. Write its values between square brackets and separate them with commas. Python counts positions from zero, so the first item is at index 0.

ExampleExerciseHint 
products = ["Notebook", "Pen", "Folder"]

print(products[0])
print(len(products))

Add a third product to this list. Then print the second name and the number of names. Run the code to check both results.

products = ["Notebook", "Pen"]

# TODO: add another product
# TODO: print the second product
# TODO: print how many products are in the list

The second item has index 1. Use len(your_list) to count the items.

Question

In your opinion, how can you get the last element of a list (assuming you don't know its length)?

items.title: Store related values in a dictionary
items.text:
A dictionary stores values under named keys. Write each key and value as a pair inside braces. Use a key in square brackets to look up its value. Dictionaries are useful when each record has named fields, such as a product and its price.

ExampleExerciseHint 
sale = {
      "product": "Notebook",
      "quantity": 3,
      "unit_price": 4.50
}

print(sale["product"])
print(sale["quantity"] * sale["unit_price"])

Run this starter code. Change the product and quantity, then add a print statement that looks up and displays the unit price. Run it again to check your changes.

sale = {"product": "Notebook", "quantity": 3, "unit_price": 4.50}

print(sale["product"])
print(sale["quantity"])
# TODO: print the unit price using its key

Look up a value with the key in square brackets, for example sale["unit_price"].

items.title: Make a decision
items.text:
An if statement runs code only when a condition is true. Use else for the alternative. The indented lines belong to the condition above them; indentation is part of Python's syntax.

ExampleExerciseHint 
total = 24

if total > 20:
    print("Large order")
else:
    print("Small order")

Run this code several times. The quantity is randomly chosen each time between 0 and 5, as the comment explains. Add an if and else so it prints In stock when the quantity is greater than zero and Out of stock otherwise. Run it several more times and observe both outcomes.

import random

# Pick a new whole number from 0 to 5 each time you run the program
quantity = random.randint(0, 5)
print(f"Quantity: {quantity}")

# TODO: print "In stock" when quantity is above 0
# TODO: otherwise print "Out of stock"

Compare quantity with zero using >. Indent the print lines underneath if and else.

items.title: Repeat work with a loop
items.text:
A for loop runs its indented code once for each item in a sequence, such as a list. The loop variable takes the value of the current item each time.

ExampleExerciseHint 
products = ["Notebook", "Pen", "Folder"]

for product in products:
    print(product)

Run the starter code. Add a for loop that prints each price in the list, then run it again and check that all three prices appear.

prices = [2.25, 4.50, 1.75]

# TODO: loop through prices and print each one

Use for price in prices: and indent the print(price) line beneath it.

items.title: Reuse steps with a function
items.text:
A function is a named set of steps. Define one with def, give it a name and any inputs in parentheses, then indent its body. Call the function by writing its name with parentheses.

ExampleExerciseHint 
def calculate_total(quantity, unit_price):
    return quantity * unit_price

total = calculate_total(3, 4.50)
print(total)

Replace pass with a print statement that greets the name. Change the name in the function call, then run the code to see your greeting.

def greet(name):
    pass  # TODO: print a greeting that includes name

greet("Sam")

Define it with def greet(name):, then put print(f"Hello, {name}!") on an indented line. Call it with greet("Sam").

items.title: Put the pieces together
items.text:
The same building blocks work together in a program. Here, a loop visits each sale, a condition keeps larger sales, and an f-string displays the result. In the next lesson, Polars will help us do similar work with columns and many rows of data.

ExampleExerciseHint 
sales = [
    {"product": "Notebook", "total": 24.00},
    {"product": "Pen", "total": 6.00},
    {"product": "Folder", "total": 18.00},
]

for sale in sales:
    if sale["total"] > 10:
        print(f"{sale['product']}: {sale['total']} euros")

Run the starter code and note which sales appear. Add another sale to the list, then change the condition from > 10 to >= 20. Run it again and check that only sales of 20 euros or more appear.

sales = [
    {"product": "Notebook", "total": 24.00},
    {"product": "Pen", "total": 6.00},
    {"product": "Folder", "total": 18.00},
]

for sale in sales:
    if sale["total"] > 10:
        print(f"{sale['product']}: {sale['total']} euros")

Each sale is a dictionary with keys product and total. Change > 10 to >= 20 to include sales that equal 20.

items.title: Where the data live
items.text:
Data warehouseData lakeBoth together

A data warehouse stores structured, organised data prepared for reporting and analysis. Teams agree on definitions, formats, and relationships before analysts query it.

Marketing example: a set of consistent campaign, customer, and sales tables used for a monthly performance report.

A data lake stores data in its original or lightly prepared form, often across many formats. Analysts and engineers decide how to interpret it when they use it.

Marketing example: raw website events, campaign exports, product reviews, and image files retained for future analysis.

Many organisations use both. They may keep raw exports in a lake, then publish quality-checked tables to a warehouse. A data lake does not automatically mean that data is messy, and a warehouse does not guarantee that every definition is correct.

Note

In this course, we'll work with CSV files. It's a very common data file format, but it isn't a database.

items.title: Relational data
items.text:
A relational database stores data in tables with defined columns. A row describes one record, and keys connect records across tables.

Table One row represents Example key campaign_sends One message sent to one customer send_id sales One transaction transaction_id website_visits One visit visit_id

For Indigo, campaign_sends.send_id can connect to sales.campaign_send_id. A key lets us combine related information without copying every campaign detail into every sale.

Relational systems work well when data has a clear structure and accurate links matter, such as orders, inventory, and campaign reporting. Examples include PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQL Server.

items.title: Non-relational data
items.text:
Non-relational databases, often grouped under the term NoSQL, do not require every record to follow the same table structure. Common models include:

DocumentKey-valueGraphWide-column

Stores records as documents, often JSON. Useful when each product or event can have a different set of attributes.

{
  "product_id": "P014",
  "name": "Active Mat 14",
  "attributes": {"colour": "blue", "material": "foam"}
}

Stores a value under a key. Useful for fast lookups such as a temporary shopping basket or a cached campaign setting.

Stores entities and the relationships between them. Useful when the connections themselves matter, such as a referral network or products frequently bought together.

Groups values by column families and is designed for large, distributed workloads such as streams of website events.

Examples include MongoDB for documents, Redis for key-value data, and Neo4j for graphs. A non-relational system is not automatically faster or more flexible for every task; its data model should fit the questions and workload.
